records.sourceFile: Association of the British Athletic Muscle Injury Classification and anatomic location with return to full training and reinjury following hamstring injury in elite soccer.pdf

paper.citation: Shamji R, James SLJ, Botchu R, Khurniawan KA, Bhogal G, Rushton A. Association of the British Athletic Muscle Injury Classification and anatomic location with return to full training and reinjury following hamstring injury in elite football. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2021;7:e001010.
paper.abstract: A retrospective cohort of 36 elite male footballers with 61 hamstring muscle injuries over eight seasons at one English club (Premier League, then Championship). Injuries extending into the intramuscular tendon (BAMIC c) were associated with a longer time to return to full training and a higher reinjury rate, and most biceps femoris reinjuries involved the distal musculotendinous junction.
paper.tldr: In one elite football club, hamstring injuries that reached the intramuscular tendon on MRI took longer to return to full training and were reinjured more often. The study is small and retrospective, so it supports closer monitoring of these injuries rather than a fixed return timeline.
paper.methods: Retrospective observational cohort using club medical records and MRI from all first-team male players with acute hamstring injuries. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded injuries with the BAMIC and recorded location; time to return to full training (TRFT) and recurrence were compared using Kruskal-Wallis and Fisher's exact tests, with descriptive analysis of location.
paper.findings: Of 61 injuries, 13 (21.3%) involved the intramuscular tendon (BAMIC c). These had a longer TRFT (mean rank 36 vs 24 days, p = 0.013) and higher reinjury (5 of 13, 38.5%, vs 12.5% without tendon involvement, p = 0.031). Overall reinjury was 16.4% (10 of 61, including 4 exacerbations), and the BAMIC-reinjury association across all grades was not significant (p = 0.083). Of the nine reinjuries to biceps femoris, five were at the distal third and distal tendon, involving both heads.
paper.limitations: Single club, retrospective design and small subgroup numbers, with only three grade 3c injuries. Repeated injuries in 12 players breaks the independence assumption. Clinicians were not blinded to MRI findings. The text reports Kruskal-Wallis mean ranks as days, while the tables give medians (for example 2c median 37 days, range 8-103); the table values are the ones reported here. Only 1.5T MRI was used and the location pattern was not tested statistically.
paper.practicalImplications: Where MRI shows intramuscular tendon involvement (BAMIC c), staff should expect a longer path to full training and plan closer reinjury monitoring. The distal biceps femoris pattern is worth noting in reinjury review but is not yet a validated decision rule.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance outcomes. Its only development relevance is for planning a player's return to training after hamstring injury, not for performance programming.
paper.rtp: The findings can inform expectations for a player with tendon involvement on MRI, but they do not set a return date: the 2c group had a median of 37 days (range 8-103) to full training, while the three 3c injuries had a median of 15 days (range 9-63). Injuries not involving the tendon also reinjured in this cohort, and the study does not validate a return-to-play criterion.

records.sourceFile: Associations between cognitive function and ACL injury-related biomechanics - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Bertozzi F, Fischer PD, Hutchison KA, Zago M, Sforza C, Monfort SM. Associations Between Cognitive Function and ACL Injury-Related Biomechanics: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2023;15(6):855-866.
paper.abstract: A systematic review of six cross-sectional studies asking whether lower baseline cognitive function is associated with ACL injury-related knee and lower-limb biomechanics during cognitively challenging sport movements. Five studies found that worse cognitive performance was associated with higher-risk biomechanics (one of these also reported an opposite direction for one variable), and one found no interaction.
paper.tldr: Across six small cross-sectional studies, athletes with weaker cognitive performance tended to show riskier knee and landing mechanics when a movement had an unexpected or dual-task demand. The evidence is associative and cannot yet be used to identify who will be injured.
paper.methods: PRISMA-P-guided systematic review of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and SciELO (1990 to June 2021), with two reviewers screening independently. Six studies were included and scored with a modified Downs and Black checklist and ROBINS-I for risk of bias. Data were synthesised narratively by cognitive domain, task and biomechanical outcome.
paper.findings: Six studies with 15 to 40 participants each (145 in total) were included. Five found worse cognitive performance associated with riskier biomechanics during cognitively challenging movements, although one of these (Giesche et al.) also found that more standing errors correlated with better working and short-term memory; the sixth (Fischer et al.) found no interaction. Herman and Barth's low-performing group had 31% higher peak vertical ground-reaction force and 4.8 degrees greater knee abduction angle than the high-performing group. Downs and Black scores were 10 to 15 of 17 and three studies had low risk of bias.
paper.limitations: The studies are cross-sectional, so no injuries were tracked and causality cannot be inferred. Sample sizes are small, 22 different cognitive tests were used, and task designs varied widely. The authors note that publication bias may inflate effects and that cognitive measures were entered together in some models, which may have reduced their individual associations. Participants with recent injury or concussion were excluded.
paper.practicalImplications: When assessing landing or cutting mechanics, consider testing with an unanticipated cue or a dual-task demand, because the review found movement patterns can change under cognitive load. Cognitive testing should not be used alone to decide who is at ACL risk on the basis of this review.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not measure performance. It suggests that adding unanticipated or dual-task demands to cutting and landing drills is a plausible way to train athletes under the cognitive load of competition, but no training intervention was tested.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It excluded participants with recent injury or concussion and includes no return-to-play data, so cognitive or biomechanical findings from these studies should not be used to clear an athlete.

records.sourceFile: Associations between hamstring fatigue and sprint kinematics during a simulated soccer match.pdf

paper.citation: Wilmes E, de Ruiter CJ, Bastiaansen BJC, Goedhart EA, Brink MS, van der Helm FCT, Savelsbergh GJP. Associations between Hamstring Fatigue and Sprint Kinematics during a Simulated Football (Soccer) Match. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: A within-subject study of ten amateur male footballers who completed a 90-minute simulated match protocol. Hamstring maximal voluntary torque, rate of torque development, EMG and 20 m sprint kinematics were measured before and after each 15-minute segment. Hamstring torque declined during the protocol, and the decline was associated with reduced knee angle at peak knee extension and an increase in peak combined hip-knee angle during sprinting.
paper.tldr: After a 90-minute football simulation, amateur players lost about 14% of hamstring isometric strength and ran slower sprints, with changes in late-swing sprint kinematics that were linked to the loss of strength. Inertial sensors could capture these changes, but the link to injury risk is untested.
paper.methods: Ten healthy amateur male footballers completed a familiarisation and an experimental session with the SAFT90 running protocol in six 15-minute segments. Before and after each segment, participants completed a 20 m sprint with five inertial sensors, then hamstring MVT and RTD tests on a dynamometer with EMG. Linear mixed models assessed time and half effects, and repeated-measures correlation assessed within-person associations between torque and kinematics.
paper.findings: Hamstring MVT fell from 105.0 to 90.3 Nm across the protocol (about 14%, Table 1), and sprint time rose from 3.58 to 3.85 s (about 7.5%, Table 2). Knee angle at peak knee extension decreased between halves (mean -2.7 degrees, p < 0.001), and hip angle at peak hip flexion decreased within and between halves. MVT loss correlated with reduced knee angle at peak knee extension (R = 0.342) and with increased peak combined angle (R = -0.251). RTD showed no consistent fatigue effect on short time intervals.
paper.limitations: Ten amateur players only, and the protocol included extra maximal sprints and strength tests that may have added fatigue. The within-half change in knee angle and the change in peak combined angle were not significant in the mixed models, so the conclusion about combined angle rests on the repeated-measures correlation. The abstract gives MVT reduction as 7.5% and sprint decline as 14.3%, which conflicts with the results and discussion (MVT about 14%, sprint time up 7.5%); the table values are reported here. About 150 of 480 RTD attempts were discarded for pre-tension or countermovement, and one or two participants showed within-person associations that contradicted the group result. No injury outcomes were collected.
paper.practicalImplications: Inertial sensors on sprinting players can detect fatigue-related changes in hamstring-relevant kinematics, so they may be worth trialling for monitoring training load. The study does not establish thresholds for action, so these measures should not be used to make substitution or injury-risk decisions yet.
paper.athleteDev: In these players, a football-specific 90-minute protocol reduced sprint performance and hamstring strength, which supports tracking sprint time and kinematics as fatigue markers during training. The sample is amateur, so the size of the effect in trained professional players may be smaller.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. Players with a hamstring injury in the previous 12 months were excluded, and the study has no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so these fatigue measures should not be used to clear an injured player.

records.sourceFile: Attention-deficit-hyperactivity disorder-related self-reported symptoms are associated with elevated concussion symptomatology.pdf

paper.citation: Bullard, L.E., Coffman, C.A., Kay, J.J.M., Holloway, J.P., Moore, R.D., Pontifex, M.B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder-Related Self-Reported Symptoms Are Associated With Elevated Concussion Symptomatology. Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology. 2022;44(2):116-126.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of 99 youths assessed during the subacute phase of concussion recovery. Inattentive ADHD symptoms, but not an ADHD diagnosis, were associated with more concussion symptoms and greater symptom severity on the SCAT5. The association was not explained by overlap between the two questionnaires or by a global executive function deficit.
paper.tldr: In youths with concussion, parent-rated inattentive ADHD symptoms were linked to higher SCAT5 symptom reports, while an ADHD diagnosis alone was not. The link did not appear to be explained by item overlap or executive function.
paper.methods: 99 participants (mean age 13.6 years; 45 female) were assessed 4 to 44 days after a physician-confirmed concussion at a pediatric sports medicine clinic. Parents or guardians, in consultation with participants, completed the ADHD-IV rating scale, the SCAT5 symptom inventory and the BRIEF executive function questionnaire. Hierarchical regression, cluster and factor analyses, and mediation analysis were used, adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, learning disorder, days since injury, loss of consciousness, prior concussions and ADHD medication.
paper.findings: Inattentive ADHD-IV percentile was associated with more SCAT5 symptoms endorsed (B = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]; R2 change = .073; p = .004) and greater symptom severity (B = 0.24, 95% CI [0.08, 0.40]; p = .003). ADHD diagnosis was not associated with symptom count (B = -1.62, p = .5) or severity (B = -4.90, p = .6), and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were not associated with either outcome. Cluster and factor analyses separated SCAT5 items from ADHD-IV items, and the BRIEF executive function composite did not significantly mediate either association.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design had no preinjury baseline, and the authors note that ADHD-related comorbidities such as depression and anxiety may account for the association. Despite the 'self-reported' title, parents completed all three questionnaires in consultation with participants, and the mediation analyses were underpowered by the authors' own estimate. The results prose repeats the diagnosis coefficient (B = -1.62) for the inattentive symptom-count model, while Table 2 gives B = 0.06; the table value is reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: When a clinician records a history of attention problems after concussion, parent-rated inattentive symptoms may add more information than a yes or no ADHD diagnosis. The authors suggest the nine inattentive items of the ADHD-IV could be used as a short subset, but this has not been tested against recovery outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not address performance training or athlete development. It cannot show how attention profiles relate to training response or performance.
paper.rtp: The study can inform how attention symptoms are considered when interpreting symptom reports in the subacute period after concussion. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing, because recovery time was not measured and the design is cross-sectional.

records.sourceFile: Biceps femoris aponeurosis size - A potential risk   factor for strain injury.pdf

paper.citation: Evangelidis PE, Massey GJ, Pain MTG, Folland JP. Biceps Femoris Aponeurosis Size: A Potential Risk Factor for Strain Injury? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2015;47(7):1383-1389.
paper.abstract: The biceps femoris long head (BFlh) proximal aponeurosis has been proposed as a hamstring strain risk factor because a small aponeurosis may concentrate strain in the surrounding muscle. In 30 healthy young men, the authors measured aponeurosis area and muscle size on MRI and isometric and eccentric knee flexor torque, and found that aponeurosis area was highly variable and unrelated to muscle size or strength.
paper.tldr: Proximal aponeurosis size varied more than fourfold between healthy young men, but it did not track muscle size or knee flexor strength. The authors suggest a small aponeurosis could be an injury risk factor, which this study did not test.
paper.methods: Thirty healthy, recreationally active men had MRI of the dominant thigh to measure BFlh proximal aponeurosis area, ACSAmax, volume and BFlh/ST tendon CSA. Isometric knee flexor torque was measured prone on a custom dynamometer at hip and knee angles of 40 and 30 degrees, and eccentric torque on an isokinetic dynamometer (hip at 60 degrees) at 50 and 350 degrees per second. Relationships were tested with Pearson correlations.
paper.findings: Aponeurosis area ranged from 7.5 to 33.5 cm2 (mean 20.4 cm2, CV 26.6%) and was not related to BFlh ACSAmax (r = 0.04, P = 0.83). The aponeurosis/muscle area ratio ranged from 0.53 to 3.09. Aponeurosis area was not related to isometric (r = 0.28, P = 0.13) or eccentric torque (r = 0.24 at both velocities, P of 0.20 or greater). By contrast, BFlh ACSAmax was related to isometric torque (r = 0.42, P less than 0.05) and to eccentric torque (r = 0.44 at 50 degrees per second and r = 0.50 at 350 degrees per second, P less than 0.05 and 0.01).
paper.limitations: Participants were healthy recreationally active men with no strength or power training, not athletes or injured players, and no injuries were recorded, so the proposed injury-risk link is untested. The knee axis was located by surface anatomy, and the authors assumed that in vivo knee flexor torque reflects BFlh force capacity. Eccentric data are from 29 participants.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and clinicians should not yet screen athletes using aponeurosis size, because the study did not link it to hamstring injury. The finding that aponeurosis size varies widely between men of similar muscle size supports that the aponeurosis is a separate anatomical characteristic to consider in future prospective research.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not show that aponeurosis size changes with training or improves strength. Its relationship with knee flexor torque was absent, so it should not be used to set training loads or to predict strength gains.
paper.rtp: Not applicable for return-to-sport decisions. The study used healthy participants without injury and did not assess rehabilitation, re-injury or post-injury aponeurosis size. Do not use the proposed injury-risk interpretation to clear or restrict an athlete.

records.sourceFile: Biceps femoris long head muscle and aponeurosis geometry in males with and without a history of hamstring strain injury.pdf

paper.citation: Lazarczuk SL, Collings TJ, Hams AH, Timmins RG, Opar DA, Edwards S, et al. Biceps femoris long head muscle and aponeurosis geometry in males with and without a history of hamstring strain injury. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34:e14619.
paper.abstract: Narrow proximal biceps femoris long head (BFlh) aponeuroses and large muscle-to-aponeurosis width ratios are proposed to raise tissue strain and hamstring strain injury risk. In 26 recreationally active males with and without a recent unilateral hamstring strain injury, the authors compared BFlh muscle and aponeurosis geometry on MRI. Previously injured limbs had larger proximal aponeurosis volumes and smaller muscle-to-aponeurosis volume ratios than control limbs, but no differences from their uninjured contralateral limbs.
paper.tldr: Recreational male athletes with a recent hamstring strain had a larger proximal BFlh aponeurosis volume and a smaller muscle-to-aponeurosis volume ratio than controls with no injury history. The difference was not seen against their own uninjured leg, and the cross-sectional design cannot show whether it preceded injury.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional retrospective analysis of 3 T MRI from both thighs of 13 males with a unilateral hamstring strain in the previous 24 months (9 to the BFlh, 4 to the medial hamstrings) and 13 males without a history, pooled from three earlier data sets. Muscle and proximal aponeurosis cross-sectional area, length, volume and interface area were segmented manually by a blinded rater. Injured limbs were compared with contralateral limbs (Wilcoxon signed-rank) and control limbs (Mann-Whitney U), with statistical parametric mapping for regional differences along the tissue length.
paper.findings: Previously injured limbs had larger proximal aponeurosis volumes than control limbs (P = .019, effect size 0.46, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.75) and smaller muscle-to-aponeurosis volume ratios (P = .029, effect size 0.43, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.73). No significant differences from uninjured contralateral limbs were found for these variables, and muscle volume, length and interface area did not differ between groups (P = .081 to 1.000 for the other comparisons). Aponeurosis and muscle volume were correlated in injured limbs (rho = 0.64, P = .022) but not in contralateral or control limbs. Regional SPM analysis found no group-by-limb interactions along the tissue length.
paper.limitations: The retrospective design cannot show whether geometric differences preceded or followed injury. Participants came from three earlier studies with different MRI parameters and slice thickness, time from injury to MRI ranged from 2 to 24 months, rehabilitation length ranged from 1 to 24 weeks, the precise injury site was unknown, and 4 of 13 injuries were not to the BFlh (results were unchanged when only the 9 BFlh injuries were analysed). The sample was powered at 0.7 to detect d = 1.0, and only proximal aponeurosis geometry was analysed.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners who measure hamstring structure should consider the whole muscle-tendon unit, not the aponeurosis alone. The finding should not yet be used to screen athletes for injury risk, because the authors note that prospective data are lacking and that the geometry may be a result of injury.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not measure strength, sprint performance or training response. It shows only a difference in tissue geometry between injured and uninjured limbs, so it should not be used to set training prescriptions.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: All injured participants had returned to pre-injury activity, and the study compared structure only, with no functional outcomes. It can inform the interpretation of imaging after hamstring injury but cannot establish whether the geometry predicts re-injury or should guide return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Biceps femoris long head stiffens after 2 weeks of training cessation in highly trained sprinters.pdf

paper.citation: Miyamoto N, Yamazaki K, Iwasaki T, Mujika I, Yamashita D, Hirata K. Biceps femoris long head stiffens after 2 weeks of training cessation in highly trained sprinters. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2024.
paper.abstract: Passive muscle stiffness has been proposed as a sprint-type hamstring strain risk factor, but the effect of short-term training cessation on it is unknown. In 28 male sprinters, the authors measured passive biceps femoris long head shear-wave speed by ultrasound elastography before and after 2 weeks of either training cessation or continued coach-prescribed training. Shear-wave speed increased after cessation and was unchanged with continued training.
paper.tldr: Two weeks without training increased passive biceps femoris long head stiffness in sprinters, while continued training left it unchanged. The study does not show whether this change raises injury risk or affects performance.
paper.methods: Twenty-eight male track-and-field sprinters were allocated (not randomised) to a training-cessation group (n = 14) or a training-continuation group (n = 14), matched on physical characteristics, event and performance level. The 2-week period began immediately after the last competition of the season. Passive BFlh shear-wave speed of the dominant leg was measured with ultrasound elastography with the hip at 70 degrees and knee fully extended, one day before and just after the 2 weeks, and analysed with a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t tests and an ANCOVA on post-intervention values.
paper.findings: Pre-intervention values did not differ between groups (P = 0.606). In the cessation group, shear-wave speed increased from 4.75 +/- 0.77 to 5.00 +/- 0.88 m/s (P less than 0.001, Cohen d 0.305). In the continuation group it changed from 4.90 +/- 0.85 to 4.93 +/- 0.85 m/s (P = 0.521). The group-by-time interaction was significant (P less than 0.001, partial eta squared 0.399), and ANCOVA showed a higher post-intervention value in the cessation group (P less than 0.001).
paper.limitations: Only males and only the dominant leg were studied, so the results may not apply to women or to the other leg. Intramuscular water content and glycogen were not controlled or measured, and only one 2-week period was tested. The authors note that the study did not assess the link between stiffness and injury incidence or sprint performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches managing a planned break or a return from illness or injury may consider that passive hamstring stiffness rose after 2 weeks of no training in this group. The authors suggest that the return to training should include work to restore muscle stiffness, but this study did not test a specific intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Passive BFlh stiffness rose during 2 weeks off training in these sprinters. The authors suggest that explosive performance is likely to improve after short-term cessation, but they did not measure any performance outcome, so use this as a reason to monitor the return to training rather than as a measured effect.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study concerns athletes without injury and does not evaluate injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-sport testing. The stiffness change is not a validated criterion for clearance, and it cannot be used to judge hamstring readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Biceps femoris muscle-tendon strain during an entire overground sprint acceleration - A biomechanical explanation for hamstring injuries in the acceleration phase.pdf

paper.citation: Astrella A, Iordanov D, De Caro D, Jiménez-Reyes P, Mendiguchia J. Biceps femoris muscle-tendon strain during an entire overground sprint acceleration: a biomechanical explanation for hamstring injuries in the acceleration phase. Sports Biomech. 2024.
paper.abstract: Hamstring injuries are common in sprinting, and most occur during acceleration. The authors estimated peak muscle-tendon strain in the hamstring muscles across the first 16 steps of a 40 m overground sprint in 21 male semi-professional soccer players, using inertial motion capture and musculoskeletal modelling. Biceps femoris long head showed the largest peak strain, which decreased as speed increased and was linked to pelvic and hip angles.
paper.tldr: In a 40 m sprint, the model-estimated peak strain in the biceps femoris long head was highest at the start and fell as speed increased, and it was linked to anterior pelvic tilt. The authors use this to propose a biomechanical reason for acceleration-phase hamstring injuries, but injuries were not measured.
paper.methods: Twenty-one male semi-professional soccer players performed two maximal 40 m sprints on natural grass. Kinematics were recorded with 17 inertial sensors at 240 Hz (Xsens MVN), and the fastest trial per player was processed in OpenSim with a scaled 37-degree-of-freedom model driven by 80 Hill-type muscle-tendon units. Peak strain of the biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus was identified for each step up to step 16. Repeated-measures ANOVA, linear mixed-effects models and simple linear regression were used.
paper.findings: Peak strain was 9.03 +/- 1.42% for the biceps femoris long head, 6.09 +/- 1.62% for the semitendinosus and 6.10 +/- 1.43% for the semimembranosus; the biceps femoris long head differed from both (P less than 0.001), and the other two did not differ (P = 0.974). Peak biceps femoris strain fell with step number (estimate -0.05 per step, P less than 0.001), and hip flexion (estimate 0.21) and knee flexion (estimate -0.11) predicted it (P less than 0.001). In the segment model only pelvis orientation was a significant predictor (estimate -0.05, P less than 0.001; femur P = 0.45), and a simple regression of the 16 step means gave r = -0.86 between anterior pelvic tilt and peak strain.
paper.limitations: Muscle activation and force were not measured, so strain values are model estimates of whole muscle-tendon length change, and the authors note that fascicle behaviour would be more appropriate. The study was a single session in semi-professional players with no injury data, players with a past hamstring strain were not excluded, and the pelvic tilt correlation uses 16 step means rather than individual data. The reported negative sign for anterior pelvic tilt is not reconciled in the text with the authors' interpretation that greater anterior tilt raises strain.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches and clinicians designing acceleration drills or hamstring prevention work could consider how pelvic tilt and hip angle change the modelled strain demand in the biceps femoris long head during early steps. These are model-based relationships in healthy players, so they suggest topics to test rather than established rules for training prescription.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings describe how the modelled hamstring strain demand changes across acceleration steps, which may inform acceleration technique discussions. Speed or performance outcomes were not measured, so the study does not show that changing pelvic tilt improves sprinting.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study tested uninjured players and did not assess rehabilitation, hamstring capacity or re-injury. The modelled strain values cannot be used to clear an athlete for sprinting or to set return-to-sprint loads.

records.sourceFile: Bidirectional interplay between traumatic brain injury and cardiovascular dysfunction in athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Kibria F, Bragina OA, Trofimov AO, Bragin D. Bidirectional Interplay Between Traumatic Brain Injury and Cardiovascular Dysfunction in Athletes. J Clin Med. 2025;14:7712.
paper.abstract: Sports-related traumatic brain injury may drive acute and chronic cardiovascular disease. The authors review epidemiological, clinical and mechanistic evidence on how brain injury affects cardiac structure and function and how cardiac disease affects brain outcomes, and they propose screening, rehabilitation and research priorities for athletes.
paper.tldr: Concussion and other sport-related brain injuries are linked to autonomic imbalance, neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy and later cardiovascular risk, and cardiac disease can in turn affect the brain. The authors propose adding neuro-cardiac checks to athlete screening, but these proposals are not yet validated in trials.
paper.methods: Narrative literature review. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for brain injury or concussion combined with sport or athlete and cardiovascular terms. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and included studies were synthesised narratively across epidemiology, acute neurocardiac complications, chronic cardiovascular sequelae and reverse brain-heart interactions. Randomised, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and case series (3 or more participants) studies and animal models were eligible.
paper.findings: The authors report that moderate-to-severe TBI carried up to a two-fold excess risk of hypertension, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction and stroke that persisted for at least a decade in larger population studies, and that higher lifetime concussion burden in former professional American-style football players was associated with a more atherogenic cardiometabolic profile and greater long-term stroke risk. They describe reduced heart rate variability and impaired baroreflex sensitivity weeks to months after concussion, and cite general (not athlete-specific) human cohorts in which 25 to 35% of patients with moderate-to-severe TBI developed QT prolongation, arrhythmia, wall motion abnormalities, troponin elevation or myocardial stunning.
paper.limitations: The review does not include a formal limitations section, and it does not apply a risk-of-bias tool or PRISMA reporting. The authors note that the scarcity of robust clinical evidence precludes definitive conclusions. Human evidence is drawn partly from non-athlete TBI cohorts and animal models, and the review was limited to English-language studies found through two databases and reference lists.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff managing athletes after concussion may consider cardiovascular symptoms and autonomic function alongside neurological recovery, since the review links brain injury to later cardiovascular risk. The proposed neuro-cardiac screening markers and HRV-guided return-to-play decisions are research proposals and are not yet validated in athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The review links athletic brain injury to changes in cardiac and autonomic function, which could affect exercise capacity, but it does not measure or prescribe training load. Use it to inform monitoring after injury rather than as a basis for training prescriptions.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review supports assessing cardiovascular and autonomic status alongside neurological recovery after concussion. It proposes HRV-guided return-to-play decisions and graded aerobic exercise, but these are not validated. It should not be used alone to clear an athlete for return to play.

records.sourceFile: Biologics for skeletal muscle healing - The role of senescence and platelet-based treatment modalities.pdf

paper.citation: Oberlohr V, Lengel H, Hambright WS, Whitney KE, Evans TA, Huard J. Biologics for Skeletal Muscle Healing: The Role of Senescence and Platelet-Based Treatment Modalities. Oper Tech Sports Med. 2020;00:150754.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers skeletal muscle repair, the role of cellular senescence in weaker regeneration with aging, and the current evidence for platelet-rich plasma and platelet-poor plasma in muscle healing. It concludes that clinical data on platelet-poor plasma are very limited and that the role of senescence in biologic treatment needs targeted study.
paper.tldr: Muscle repair slows with age as satellite cells fail and senescent cells add pro-inflammatory and fibrotic signals. PRP has short-term clinical signals, but PPP has almost no in vivo or clinical testing, so neither is ready to guide routine muscle-injury care.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors summarise 9 registered clinical trials (results posted for 4), 5 in vitro studies and 10 preclinical in vivo studies of PRP or PPP. The literature search is described only in general terms, with no databases, dates or screening criteria reported.
paper.findings: Aging reduces satellite cell number and function, and senescent cells add inflammatory and fibrotic signals; the review also notes a possible protective role for early fibro-adipogenic progenitor senescence. In clinical trials, PRP was linked to short-term pain improvement where pain was reported (one of these was a temporomandibular disorder trial), and one trial in athletes with acute hamstring strain found faster return to play with PRP than PPP. In vitro, all 5 PRP studies reported increased myogenic proliferation, and none of the 10 preclinical studies used PPP as the investigational treatment.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no stated appraisal of study quality and no pooled analysis. Results were posted for only 4 of 9 registered trials, and most mechanistic evidence comes from cell and animal models that may not transfer to human muscle injury. The authors state that the studies used different treatments and outcomes, so no concise conclusion on PRP in skeletal muscle could be drawn.
paper.practicalImplications: When discussing PRP for a muscle strain, tell athletes that most of the evidence comes from laboratory and animal work and from a few clinical trials of mixed design. Do not plan around PPP for muscle injury: none of the 10 preclinical studies used it as the investigational treatment, and only 2 registered clinical trials included it (one as the comparator to PRP). Treat the senescence-targeting and customized PRP ideas as future research rather than current practice.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not address performance enhancement. Its athlete-relevant material is limited to injury recovery, so it cannot support using PRP or PPP to improve strength or training capacity in healthy athletes.
paper.rtp: Use with caution. One trial in athletes with acute hamstring strain reported faster return to play with PRP than PPP, and a randomized trial in acute muscle tears reported faster return to play with PRP than no injection, although the review notes the difference was not significant at 2-year follow-up. These trials are few and varied, so they cannot set return-to-sport criteria or a PRP-based timeline.

records.sourceFile: Biomechanical impact of soccer shoe outsole design on knee joint during cutting movements.pdf

paper.citation: Wang D, Sun D, Gu Y. Biomechanical impact of soccer shoe outsole design on knee joint during cutting movements. Footwear Science. 2025;17(S1):S264-S265.
paper.abstract: This conference abstract compares two soccer shoe outsole designs with 8 and 9 forefoot studs during sidestep cutting in 17 healthy male players. The 9-stud shoe gave more traction and higher knee valgus and internal rotation moments, while peak vertical ground reaction force did not differ.
paper.tldr: In a small lab study, a soccer shoe with nine forefoot studs gave more traction and higher knee valgus and internal rotation moments during sidestep cutting than one with eight. The study is a short abstract that did not measure injury, so it cannot say whether this changes injury risk.
paper.methods: Seventeen healthy male soccer players performed 45-degree dribbling sidestep cuts in two shoe conditions, presented in random order: 8 studs and 9 studs in the forefoot, with other shoe features reported as similar. Motion was captured with 12 Vicon cameras at 250 Hz, ground reaction forces with a Kistler force plate at 1000 Hz, and knee moments were modelled in Visual3D. Paired t-tests (alpha 0.05) compared the conditions.
paper.findings: The 9-stud shoe (ATM2) had a higher dynamic traction coefficient than the 8-stud shoe (0.34 vs 0.27, p<0.05). Its knee valgus moment (0.98 vs 0.83 N·m·BW-1) and knee internal rotation moment (1.16 vs 0.79 N·m·BW-1) were also higher (both p<0.05). Peak vertical ground reaction force, knee varus, external rotation, flexion and extension moments did not differ significantly (Table 1).
paper.limitations: The text is a two-page abstract, so effect sizes, participant characteristics, trial numbers and full methods are not reported. The abstract does not state outright which condition is ATM1 or ATM2; this record assumes ATM1 is the 8-stud shoe and ATM2 the 9-stud shoe, following the order the conditions are listed. The discussion says the 9-stud shoe had a larger effect on knee valgus, varus and rotation angles, but no angle values appear in the results or Table 1, and its claim that more studs improve stability was not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: More forefoot studs appear to add traction, but in this sample they also raised knee valgus and internal rotation moments during sidestep cuts. Staff choosing stud layouts should weigh the traction gain against the knee load increase, and the authors advise players to consider their own needs and use scenarios. The study did not include injured players, so it does not show that either layout is safer for a player with a knee history.
paper.athleteDev: A forefoot stud layout that adds traction may also raise knee loads during sidestep cuts. Judge stud configuration against the cutting demands of the player and surface, and check the trade-off on the player's own movement rather than by traction alone.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study tested healthy players only and did not measure injured knees or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform footwear decisions after a knee injury.

records.sourceFile: Brachial plexus injuries in the contact athlete - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Windmueller RA, Gbayisomore OO, Mead RL, Desai MJ, Bowman EN. Brachial plexus injuries in the contact athlete: a narrative review. Annals of Joint. 2025;10:18.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of brachial plexus injuries (BPIs) in contact athletes, from transient neuropraxia ('burners' or 'stingers') to neurotmesis. The review covers epidemiology, injury mechanisms, diagnosis, treatment and return to sport, based on an English-language literature search from inception to October 2024.
paper.tldr: Most contact-athlete brachial plexus injuries are transient neuropraxias that resolve within minutes to hours. Symptoms lasting beyond 2 to 3 weeks warrant further evaluation for axonal injury.
paper.methods: Narrative literature review, not systematic. Searches of PubMed, Cochrane Review and Google Scholar covered English-language sources from inception to October 2024, using key terms; three co-authors selected sources by consensus and reference lists were checked.
paper.findings: Neuropraxia is common, with a 49% to 65% prevalence among career football players in cross-sectional studies. In a 2015 to 2019 NFL epidemiological study, the average single-season stinger risk was about 3.74%, and 76% of affected players missed no time. Repeated burners have been linked to a smaller Torg ratio, but no prospective or retrospective study shows that repeated burners increase the risk of axonal injury.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and has no reported quality appraisal, and the literature it draws on is weighted toward football and rugby in English-speaking countries. Severe injuries are covered mainly by small case series, and there are no randomized trials on rehabilitation, return to sport or prevention.
paper.practicalImplications: For a contact athlete with a burner or stinger, the review supports concussion screening and checking for full return to neurologic baseline and pain-free neck and shoulder motion before return. Symptoms beyond about 2 weeks or recurrent burners call for further evaluation (EMG or nerve conduction, MRI or CT myelogram), and inability to hold the shoulder protracted or scapular winging should raise suspicion of root avulsion. Neck rolls and collars are empirically recommended in the absence of harm; lab studies show they reduce hyperextension but not passive lateral flexion.
paper.athleteDev: The review gives no performance or training guidance. Its use for performance staff is in referral: arm weakness, burning pain or symptoms that persist beyond the expected window should go to medical staff, not be trained through.
paper.rtp: Supports same-game or same-week return for typical neuropraxic burners once neurologic baseline and pain-free neck and shoulder motion are restored, after concussion evaluation. It cannot be used to set return dates for axonotmesis or neurotmesis, where timelines depend on injury grade and nerve regeneration of about 1 mm per day, and the review says return-to-sport outcomes need further study.

records.sourceFile: Can human growth hormone accelerate tendon and ligament injury recovery.pdf

paper.citation: Baumgarten KM, Sandhurst ES, Sun H. Can human growth hormone accelerate tendon and ligament injury recovery? Sports Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: Basic science study of human tendon and ligament fibroblasts from 24 patients exposed to human growth hormone (HGH) in single-dose and sustained-dose models. HGH did not improve cell proliferation or collagen production in most conditions, and several doses reduced proliferation, so the authors do not support HGH for accelerating injury recovery.
paper.tldr: In a cell culture study of human tendon and ligament fibroblasts, growth hormone did not increase cell growth or collagen production and reduced growth at several doses. This is laboratory evidence only and cannot show what happens to an injured athlete.
paper.methods: Ligament fibroblasts were harvested from the ACL during knee arthroplasty (13 patients) and tendon fibroblasts from hamstring autograft excess during ACL reconstruction (11 patients). Cells were treated with HGH in a single-dose model and a sustained-dose model (re-dosed on days 2, 4 and 6), with MTS proliferation assays at days 4 and 7 and Picrosirius Red collagen staining at day 14. One-way ANOVA compared each dose with untreated controls, and the 100 ng/mL dose was re-tested with 18 treated wells against 6 controls.
paper.findings: Single-dose HGH reduced day-7 ligament fibroblast proliferation at 100 pg/mL (90.9%, p<0.01), 1 ng/mL (89.7%), 1 µg/mL (90.4%) and 10 µg/mL (90.7%), and tendon fibroblast proliferation at 100 pg/mL (94.5%), 1 ng/mL (93.7%) and 10 ng/mL (96.7%, p=0.03). In the sustained model, ligament cells grew more at day 4 at 100 ng/mL (107.7%, p=0.03) and 10 µg/mL (104.6%, p<0.01), tendon cells grew less at day 4 at 1 µg/mL and 100 µg/mL, and no dose improved proliferation at day 7. When 100 ng/mL was re-tested with 18 treated wells, single-dose proliferation was not improved (ligament 96.1%, p=0.33; tendon 99.5%, p=0.63), sustained-dose proliferation was lower (ligament day 7, 95.1%, p<0.01; tendon day 4, 95.6%, p=0.03), and collagen production was similar or lower than controls, significantly so in ligament cells at 1 ng/mL (93.5%, p=0.05).
paper.limitations: Cell culture cannot reproduce pulsatile pituitary release or systemic HGH effects, and the study tested only paracrine exposure. Donor cells came from patients of different ages and from two tissue sources, which the authors note as a confounder, and there was no tissue mechanical or in vivo outcome. The Methods give a dose range to 100 µg/mL while the Abstract gives 10 µg/mL, and the Abstract names 100 ng/mL as the only sustained-dose ligament concentration that was similar or better, although the Results also report a day-4 increase at 10 µg/mL (104.6%). Pfizer donated the HGH, and the sponsors had no stated role in design or reporting.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not use this study to justify HGH for tendon or ligament injury recovery, and do not treat it as evidence that HGH slows healing either. The paper notes HGH is not FDA-approved for injury recovery, so staff should not plan rehabilitation or return timelines around it.
paper.athleteDev: This in vitro work gives no basis for using HGH to improve tendon or ligament capacity or performance in athletes. Staff should base any recovery or performance plan on tested interventions rather than this cell study.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It used fibroblasts from non-athlete surgical patients in culture and measured no clinical healing, strength, or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Can the workload-injury                        relationship be moderated by improved strength, speed     and                repeatedsprint     qualities_  - Copy.pdf

paper.citation: Malone S, Hughes B, Doran DA, Collins K, Gabbett TJ. Can the workload-injury relationship be moderated by improved strength, speed and repeated-sprint qualities? J Sci Med Sport. 2018.
paper.abstract: Observational cohort study of 40 male amateur hurling players over two seasons, linking session-RPE workload, time-loss injuries and physical qualities (relative strength, 5- to 20-m sprint speed and repeated-sprint ability). Moderate weekly loads were linked to lower injury odds, large week-to-week load changes to higher odds, and stronger, faster and better repeated-sprint players to lower odds of injury at higher loads.
paper.tldr: In 40 amateur hurling players over two seasons, moderate weekly loads carried lower injury odds, and players with greater strength, faster sprint times and better repeated-sprint ability tolerated higher loads with lower odds of injury. These are observational associations from one team, not tested causes.
paper.methods: Observational cohort of 40 male amateur hurling players from one team over two seasons. Weekly training load was session-RPE multiplied by duration, with time-loss injuries (missed day or more) recorded. Relative lower-body strength was tested by 3RM trap-bar deadlift, sprint speed over 5, 10 and 20 m, and repeated-sprint ability (6 x 35 m, total time). Weekly load, ACWR, week-to-week change, and physical qualities were modelled against injury with polynomial regression, with odds ratios against quartile reference groups and VIF checks for multicollinearity.
paper.findings: Moderate weekly loads of 1400 to 1900 AU had lower injury odds than loads of 1200 AU or less in the pre-season (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.66) and in-season (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.82). Large absolute week-to-week changes of 1000 AU or more had higher odds (pre-season OR 5.58, in-season OR 4.98). At weekly loads of 1750 AU or more, slower 5-m (OR 3.11), 10-m (OR 3.45) and 20-m (OR 3.12) times were linked to higher injury odds. For repeated-sprint total time at the same loads, the authors report an OR of 5.55 (95% CI 3.98 to 7.94) and describe better repeated-sprint players as at reduced risk. An ACWR of 0.90 to 1.30 was described as protective, and ACWR explained 60% of the variance in injury.
paper.limitations: Single team, 40 players and 93 injuries, with no interaction test and no adjustment for previous injury, age, soreness, sleep or other factors the authors name. The Abstract gives height 184.2 cm and mass 82.6 ± 4.7 kg, while the Methods give 182.2 cm and 81.3 ± 3.7 kg; the Abstract's 5-m and 10-m confidence intervals differ from Table 2 (5-m 2.23 to 3.87, 10-m 2.71 to 4.12); and in Table 1 some odds ratios have confidence intervals that exclude 1 but p values above 0.4 (for example OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.29, p = 0.459). The repeated-sprint OR of 5.55 is reported beside a 'reduced risk' statement without a clearly stated reference group.
paper.practicalImplications: In this amateur squad, absolute week-to-week changes of 1000 AU or more and very low weekly loads (1200 AU or less) carried higher injury odds than moderate weekly loads of 1400 to 1900 AU, so these session-RPE bands are a starting point for flags only in similar squads. Strength, 5- to 20-m sprint and repeated-sprint testing can help identify players who had higher injury odds at high loads, but the study did not test whether improving these qualities lowers injury risk.
paper.athleteDev: Use strength, sprint and repeated-sprint results to identify players who may tolerate high weekly loads or large load changes less well, and track weekly load changes alongside them. The authors' claim that improving these qualities will reduce injury risk was not tested, and the cut-offs are cohort-specific; the authors recommend testing the model in other teams and sports.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It models the risk of injury occurring in training and matches, not recovery from injury or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Cannabinoid therapy in athletics - A review of current cannabis research to evaluate potential real-world cannabinoid applications in sport.pdf

paper.citation: Thompson ES, Alcorn J, Neary JP. Cannabinoid Therapy in Athletics: A Review of Current Cannabis Research to Evaluate Potential Real-World Cannabinoid Applications in Sport. Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: This narrative review evaluates published cannabis research for its possible uses in athletes. It covers the endocannabinoid system, inflammation, pain and opioid-sparing effects, concussion, mental health, performance, product forms and administration routes, and regulation. The authors note that elite athletes are under-represented in cannabis research and that sport policies are inconsistent.
paper.tldr: Athletes are turning to cannabinoids for inflammation, pain, sleep, concussion and mood, but the human athlete evidence is thin and inconsistent. Use this review to frame questions about product, dose and route, not as a case for use.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Medline, EMBASE, EBSCOhost, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar using keywords and subject headings, and also checked reference lists, meta-analyses and clinical trial registries. No inclusion criteria, screening process or quality appraisal are reported.
paper.findings: Human results are mixed. In trained people, one 60 mg oral CBD study found lower myoglobin than placebo only in more advanced athletes, with no effect on creatine kinase, strength, power or endurance; another 150 mg CBD study found no effect on muscle damage markers, as the review reports them. A 10 mg THC edible had no ergogenic or ergolytic effect in habitually active adults, while inhaled THC impaired vigorous exercise performance in another trial and inhaled CBD without THC did not.
paper.limitations: The narrative design gives no reproducible search strategy or quality appraisal, so the weight given to each study cannot be checked. Most of the mechanistic and anti-concussion evidence is preclinical or drawn from non-athlete populations, and the review describes the same 60 mg CBD trial inconsistently (the inflammation section says it reduced creatine kinase and myoglobin; the recovery section says only myoglobin fell, in advanced athletes, with no change in creatine kinase). The glossary has errors (for example, IL-2 is defined as interleukin-6 and GABA as G-protein coupled receptors).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should ask what product, cannabinoid content and dose an athlete uses, and whether it has third-party testing, because the review documents CBD products that contain THC or are mislabelled. Because the athlete evidence does not show a recovery or performance benefit, CBD should not be presented as a proven recovery aid, and athletes should check their league or testing body's rules first (WADA still bans THC but not CBD).
paper.athleteDev: The review does not show a performance gain from cannabinoids. THC trials range from no effect to impaired vigorous exercise performance, and CBD trials show no clear change in strength, power or endurance. The review also notes, without testing it for CBD, that anti-inflammatory agents taken close to resistance training may blunt adaptation, so timing should be considered.
paper.rtp: The review does not show that cannabinoids speed return to sport after injury or concussion. Its concussion and pain sections rest mainly on rodent, in vitro and mechanistic work, and the one cited human concussion study reported lower symptom burden in weeks 3 and 4 with no change in recovery time. It should not guide clearance, medication or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Cardiac cycle timing and contractility following acute sport-related concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Singh J, Ellingson CJ, Ellingson CA, Scott P, Neary JP. Cardiac cycle timing and contractility following acute sport-related concussion. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Twelve varsity athletes were assessed within 5 days of a diagnosed sport-related concussion and compared with their own pre-season baseline. A non-invasive sternal sensor recorded one minute of supine cardiac cycle data. Systolic time decreased and atrial contractile force increased during the acute phase, while the other timing and contractility measures did not change significantly.
paper.tldr: In 12 varsity athletes tested within 5 days of concussion, a one-minute resting sensor recording showed a shorter systolic time and higher atrial contractile force than their own baseline. The sample is small and uncontrolled, so this is a signal to watch, not a diagnostic marker.
paper.methods: Within-subject comparison of 12 concussed athletes with their own pre-season baseline, using follow-up at 3 ± 1 days post-injury. A sensor placed over the sternum on a single adhesive ECG electrode recorded one minute of supine data, from which cardiac timing intervals and twist and atrial contractile force were derived. Paired changes were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
paper.findings: Median systolic time fell from 298 ms (IQR 42) at baseline to 276 ms (IQR 32) during the acute phase (p = 0.034). Median atrial systole force rose from 10 mG (IQR 6) to 13 mG (IQR 5) (p = 0.013). Heart rate, isovolumic times, diastole, twist force and the performance indices did not change significantly.
paper.limitations: The study has no control group and only 12 athletes (3 female, 9 male). Thirteen variables were compared with no stated correction for multiple testing. The discussion proposes reduced stroke volume and cerebral perfusion changes, but neither was measured. The methods describe repeated follow-up visits, yet only acute-phase results are reported. The sensor maker, LLA Technologies, funded the work through a Mitacs grant and its proprietary algorithm extracted the cardiac features.
paper.practicalImplications: This study alone does not show that a resting sensor recording can screen for cardiac problems after concussion, or that it would change return-to-play decisions. The authors argue for baseline cardiac testing in competitive athletes. Any change in an athlete should be read against that athlete's own baseline.
paper.athleteDev: No performance outcomes were measured. The study can inform only how to read resting cardiac sensor data in an athlete who has had a concussion: compare the athlete with their own baseline.
paper.rtp: The study cannot be used to set return-to-sport timing or clearance. It reports only the acute phase (within 5 days) and does not show whether the cardiac changes resolve, persist, or relate to symptoms.

records.sourceFile: Cardiovascular effects of doping substances, commonly prescribed medications and ergogenic aids in relation to sports - EAPC Position Paper.pdf

paper.citation: Adami PE, Koutlianos N, Baggish A, Bermon S, Cavarretta E, Deligiannis A, et al. Cardiovascular effects of doping substances, commonly prescribed medications and ergogenic aids in relation to sports: a position statement of the sport cardiology and exercise nucleus of the European Association of Preventive Cardiology. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2022;29(3):559-575.
paper.abstract: The use of substances and medications with potential cardiovascular effects among people practising sport and physical activity has increased in recent years. This position paper reviews recent literature and updates a 2006 statement on the adverse cardiovascular effects of doping substances, commonly prescribed medications and ergogenic aids in sport and exercise. The cardiovascular effect depends on the type of substance, the amount, the duration of use and the individual response.
paper.tldr: A European cardiology position statement that reviews heart risks from doping agents, prescribed medicines and sports supplements. It documents the most serious heart harms for anabolic steroids, while for many legal supplements it lists the cardiovascular effects as unknown.
paper.methods: Expert position statement by the EAPC sport cardiology and exercise section. The authors undertook a comprehensive review of published evidence and assessed pharmacology, cardiovascular mechanisms, effects on exercise performance and benefit-risk for each substance group. The text does not describe a search strategy or an evidence-grading system.
paper.findings: Anabolic steroid users show increased cardiomyopathy and left ventricular dysfunction, and the statement estimates mortality 6 to 20 times higher than in clean athletes, with around 30% of these deaths attributed to cardiovascular causes. Stimulants, beta-2 agonists and clenbuterol are linked to arrhythmias, hypertension and tachycardia, and caffeine intakes above about 9 mg/kg raise side-effect risk. Energy drinks, ephedra-contaminated products and nicotine are linked to arrhythmias, vasoconstriction and hypertension, while creatine has no well-established cardiovascular effects but has case reports of thrombosis, atrial fibrillation and sudden death.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative expert statement, not a systematic review, and its search and evidence-grading methods are not described. Many anabolic steroid studies are small, rely on self-reported dose and duration, and involve several substances at once, so effects cannot be attributed to a single agent. Several agents discussed, including SARMs, peptides, cobalt and gene doping, have little or no human cardiovascular data.
paper.practicalImplications: The statement advises physicians to discuss substance and supplement risks openly with athletes, to recommend supplements only for a demonstrated need such as a deficiency, and to favour products from established manufacturers because contamination rates of 12% to 58% are reported. Athletes with established heart disease should consult a physician before using any supplement or ergogenic aid. Before prescribing beta-blockers or antiarrhythmics to an athlete, it advises maximal exercise testing before prescription and during up-titration, and a TUE may be needed in some sports.
paper.athleteDev: The statement reports little or no performance evidence for growth hormone, inhaled beta-2 agonists and PDE5 inhibitors in normoxia, while anabolic steroids, blood doping and rhEPO show gains in small controlled trials alongside serious cardiovascular risk. Among legal supplements it lists caffeine, creatine, carbohydrate, beta-alanine, bicarbonate, nitrate and protein as having reliable performance evidence, and notes that caffeine side effects become more common above about 9 mg/kg.
paper.rtp: The statement does not set return-to-sport criteria. For returning athletes, its relevant points are that anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs raise bleeding risk in contact and collision sports, and that athletes with established heart disease should consult a physician before resuming supplements or ergogenic aids.

records.sourceFile: Cervical Intervertebral Disc Degeneration and Low Cervical Extension Independently Associated With a History of Stinger Syndrome.pdf

paper.citation: Hakkaku T, Nakazato K, Koyama K, Kouzaki K, Hiranuma K. Cervical Intervertebral Disc Degeneration and Low Cervical Extension Independently Associated With a History of Stinger Syndrome. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;5(11):2325967117735830.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined whether cervical intervertebral disc degeneration (CIDD) and neck function are related to a history of stinger syndrome in Japanese collegiate football players. Forty-nine players were divided into stinger and control groups, and CIDD was assessed by T2-weighted MRI, with range of motion and isometric strength also measured. CIDD was more common in the stinger group, and cervical extension range of motion was lower, and both were independently associated with stinger history in logistic regression.
paper.tldr: In 49 collegiate football players, a stinger in the past year was linked to disc degeneration on MRI and to reduced neck extension range. The design is cross-sectional, so these are associations and not predictors of future stingers.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study of 49 male first-division collegiate football players. Stinger syndrome was identified by questionnaire, interview and health record review, and players were grouped into stinger (n=19) and control (n=30). Five cervical discs (C2/C3 to C6/C7) were scored on T2-weighted MRI by two blinded spine surgeons, and neck range of motion (goniometer) and handheld dynamometer strength were measured after the season. Group differences were tested with t tests and chi-square, and logistic regression was used for adjusted associations.
paper.findings: CIDD was seen in 13 of 19 players with stinger history (68%) and 9 of 30 controls (30%), P < .01, and 14 of 23 defensive players versus 5 of 26 offensive players had stingers. Cervical extension range was lower in the stinger group (50.9 vs 60.2 degrees, P < .01, d = 0.83), and neck isometric strength did not differ. In logistic regression, CIDD (adjusted OR 5.58, 95% CI 1.43 to 21.76) and extension range (adjusted OR 0.93 per degree, 95% CI 0.87 to 0.99) were independently associated with stinger history.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot show causality, and only 49 players (19 with stinger history) were studied. Stinger history depends on questionnaire, interview and records, and neck function was measured after the season, not before the stingers occurred. Table 7 gives the crude OR for CIDD as 5.06 with a 95% CI of 1.46 to 5.06, where the upper limit equals the estimate, so this entry looks wrong. The methods say 'lumbar disc degeneration was graded' with the Pfirrmann scale, which appears to be a labelling slip since the discussion states the lumbar scale was applied to cervical discs, and MRI used a low-field 0.3-T unit.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that pre-season checks include neck extension range and MRI or physical examination, since both features were linked to stinger history. If reduced extension range or disc degeneration is found, the authors suggest coaching a head-up tackling technique, but this study does not show that doing so prevents stingers. Neck strength testing alone did not separate the groups, so it should not be relied on for screening.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance. Its findings concern neck injury history and neck function, so it cannot be used to judge playing ability.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to play. It is cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether low extension range or disc degeneration predicts recurrent stingers or affects the timing of a return to play.

records.sourceFile: Changes in health related parameters associated with sports performance enhancement drugs.pdf

paper.citation: Wiacek M, Trąbka B, Tomasiuk R, Zubrzycki IZ. Changes in Health-Related Parameters Associated with Sports Performance Enhancement Drugs. Int J Sports Med. 2022.
paper.abstract: Eight male bodybuilders were measured monthly over a six-month competition preparation that included self-administered anabolic steroids, growth hormone, fat-burning drugs and other agents. Lipids, liver enzymes, bilirubin, urea and body composition were compared with a NHANES-based reference sample. The authors conclude that the drugs had no immediate detrimental impact on the parameters studied, while acknowledging the small sample and unverified drug quality.
paper.tldr: In eight drug-using bodybuilders, AST, ALT, bilirubin and BUN were higher and HDL-C lower than in the reference sample during a six-month preparation, although the authors judge most values physiologically acceptable. The study is too small and uncontrolled to show long-term safety.
paper.methods: Analysis of competitor medical notes and monthly fasting blood tests and DXA body composition in eight male bodybuilders (age 30 to 35, 97 to 110 kg) who self-administered drugs during 6 months of preparation. Values were compared with 100 NHANES men aged 30 to 35 using Welch ANOVA over time and Games-Howell post hoc tests.
paper.findings: Body mass rose from about 105 to 109 kg and body fat fell over the preparation. Table 2 (column labeled Month 1) marks total cholesterol (4.15 vs 5.17 mmol/L), HDL-C (0.52 vs 1.18 mmol/L), AST (1.60 vs 0.45 µkat/L), ALT (1.99 vs 0.53 µkat/L), bilirubin (6.83 vs 4.63 µmol/L), BUN (8.29 vs 4.8 mmol/L) and body fat (7.62% vs 26.56%) as different from the reference sample, while TG and LDL-C were not marked. The authors describe AST and ALT as in the high range throughout, BUN moving between desirable and high, and mean BMD of 1.34 vs 1.44 g/cm2 in the first and sixth months without a statistical test.
paper.limitations: Eight men, no untreated control, unverified drug quality, dosing given as ranges, and a general-population NHANES reference rather than matched athletes. The text is internally inconsistent: the Results say all parameters except LDL-C were in normal ranges while later sections place AST and ALT in the high range and BUN in the high range, the TG section states no significant TC difference although Table 2 and the TC section report one, and Table 2 is labeled Month 1 while presented as the overall comparison. The BMD change rests on two time points with no test.
paper.practicalImplications: In this group the markers that sat furthest from reference values were AST, ALT, HDL-C and BUN, so these are the ones the data flag for athletes known to use these drugs. The study does not show the drugs are safe, and the authors state long-term effects are not established, so it should not be used to reassure athletes about risk.
paper.athleteDev: The study has no direct training application because it describes health markers during drug-assisted preparation rather than training effects. Performance staff should not read the body mass or body fat changes as a training response, since drug use, diet and training were not separated.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport or clearance decisions: there were no injured athletes and no function or return outcomes. The conclusion of no immediate harm should not be used as a clearance standard for athletes with a drug-use history.

records.sourceFile: Changes in muscle architecture of     biceps femoris induced by eccentric strength training with Nordic    hamstring  exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Alonso-Fernandez D, Docampo-Blanco P, Martinez-Fernandez J. Changes in muscle architecture of biceps femoris induced by eccentric strength training with nordic hamstring exercise. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017;1-7.
paper.abstract: This single-group study followed 23 recreational men through 8 weeks of nordic hamstring exercise and 4 weeks of detraining, measuring biceps femoris long head architecture by 2D ultrasound at three time points. Fascicle length increased and pennation angle decreased after training, and both moved back toward baseline after detraining. The authors conclude that NHE changes this muscle's architecture in ways that may matter for injury prevention and rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: Eight weeks of nordic hamstring exercise lengthened biceps femoris fascicles and lowered pennation angle in recreational men, and four weeks off partly reversed these changes. Architecture is a structural marker, so the study does not show fewer injuries.
paper.methods: Twenty-three men with no lower-limb injury in the prior 12 months completed baseline testing, 8 weeks of progressive NHE (2 to 3 sessions per week, 10 to 20 minutes each), and 4 weeks of detraining. Fascicle length, relative fascicle length, muscle thickness and pennation angle were measured at rest by 2D B-mode ultrasound and compared across time with one-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
paper.findings: Fascicle length rose from 8.17 to 10.12 cm by week 9 (+23.9%, d=2.28, P<.001) and fell to 8.90 cm by week 13 (P<.001 vs week 9). Pennation angle fell from 14.74 to 12.55 degrees (-14.8%, P<.001) and rose to 13.71 degrees after detraining, while muscle thickness rose from 2.09 to 2.25 cm (+7.7%, P<.001) and returned to 2.10 cm (P<.05 vs week 9).
paper.limitations: No control group, so changes could partly reflect repeated testing or time, and fascicle length depends on an estimation equation whose reliability was tested in 12 people. The Table 3 caption labels the values as mean±SEM, but the spread (for example 8.17±1.83 cm) looks like SD for n=23, so check dispersion before quoting.
paper.practicalImplications: Partner-assisted NHE, needing no equipment beyond a partner holding the heels, changed fascicle length and pennation angle in recreational men within 8 weeks. Because these changes partly reversed within 4 weeks off eccentric work, the authors suggest continued exposure is needed to keep them.
paper.athleteDev: NHE is an accessible eccentric hamstring stimulus, and this protocol used 2 to 3 sessions per week of 10 to 20 minutes. The study did not measure strength, speed or sprint performance, so it shows no performance benefit.
paper.rtp: The study cannot serve as a return-to-sport standard because it had no injured athletes and no function or reinjury measures. The authors' suggestion that architectural change may help rehabilitation is untested in this sample.

records.sourceFile: Chronic changes in muscle architecture and aponeurosis structure following calf muscle strain injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Nielsen LB, Svensson RB, Fredskild NU, Mertz KH, Magnusson SP, Kjaer M, et al. Chronic changes in muscle architecture and aponeurosis structure following calf muscle strain injuries. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;1-13.
paper.abstract: Ten people with a previous chronic calf strain had their medial gastrocnemius studied with dynamic ultrasound and EMG, comparing the injured and uninjured calf. The injured distal muscle showed a larger pennation angle increase during contraction, shorter fascicles, a curved fascicle shape, a thicker aponeurosis and higher relative soleus activity. The authors conclude that some distal fibers may not be actively engaged after a strain injury and that the aponeurosis changes are long-lasting.
paper.tldr: Long after a calf strain, the injured medial gastrocnemius showed steeper, curved fascicles during contraction and a thicker aponeurosis than the uninjured side. The study is small and cross-sectional, so it describes the injured calf rather than proving permanent change.
paper.methods: Ten participants with chronic calf strain injuries (3 women, 7 men) had 2D ultrasound of the medial gastrocnemius at three ankle angles and during unilateral heel rise, with fascicle length and pennation angle measured by an automated tracking macro, plus EMG of the gastrocnemius and soleus. Injured and uninjured sides were compared with repeated-measures mixed models and paired t-tests.
paper.findings: At the most distal fascicle, pennation angle rose 18.9 degrees from relaxed to peak contraction on the injured side and 6.6 degrees on the uninjured side (difference 12.4 degrees, P=.01), with a similar pattern at the next fascicle (difference 12.1 degrees, P=.005). Fascicles were shorter on the injured side at the central distal site on still images (11.0 mm, P=.004) and at the most distal fascicle on video (11.9 mm, P=.009), and the aponeurosis was thicker on the injured side distally (5.9 mm, P=.0003) and at mid-belly sites in six participants (3.1 to 3.5 mm, P=.04). Soleus EMG during heel rise was higher on the injured side (P=.02) and the soleus-to-gastrocnemius ratio was higher (P=.04), while gastrocnemius EMG and MVC strength did not differ.
paper.limitations: No healthy control group, only 10 participants (six for mid-belly video), and time since injury that varied widely (mean 47 months, SD 25). The Discussion calls the changes possibly permanent, but one cross-sectional visit cannot show that, the linear fascicle estimate underestimates the curved injured fascicles, and EMG electrodes sat at mid-belly rather than the injured distal site.
paper.practicalImplications: Long-standing calf strains may leave altered muscle and aponeurosis structure, so rehabilitation planning should not assume full structural recovery once the injury has settled. This is a hypothesis from one cross-sectional study and has not been tested in a trial.
paper.athleteDev: This study has no training application: it measured calf structure and muscle activity in people with long-standing strains and tested no training intervention. The authors note it is unknown whether eccentric training would lengthen the distal fascicles of the injured muscle.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: no function, strength or reinjury outcome was measured, and the injuries were years old. The proposed link between altered fascicles and reinjury risk is the authors' hypothesis.

records.sourceFile: Classification of myo-connective tissue injuries for severity grading and return to play prediction - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Fontanier V, Bruchard A, Tremblay M, Mohammed R, da Silva-Oolup S, Suri-Chilana M, et al. Classification of myo-connective tissue injuries for severity grading and return to play prediction: a scoping review. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review searched Medline and SPORTDiscus from 2010 to April 2022 for classifications of acute non-contact muscle injuries in sporting adults. From 13,426 records, 37 studies were included, identifying 24 classifications, most developed for hamstring or lower-limb injuries. Time to return to play was the most reported outcome, and the authors conclude that the evidence is inconsistent and that classifications are not sufficient to predict return to play.
paper.tldr: Muscle injury grading systems such as BAMIC, modified Peetrons, Munich and Cohen are widely used, but evidence that their grades predict return-to-play time is weak and inconsistent. Use them to describe injuries and to communicate with the medical team, not to set an individual return date.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. Medline (PubMed) and SPORTDiscus were searched from 1 January 2010 to 19 April 2022 using MeSH and free-text terms for muscle injury and classification. Included studies were English-language, peer-reviewed, in sporting adults aged 18 or older with acute non-contact muscle or tendon injury, and reported a severity grading applicable to prognosis. Pairs of reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts, one reviewer extracted data and a second verified it, and findings were synthesized qualitatively.
paper.findings: Of 37 included studies, 24 classifications with reported outcomes were identified, and the six most cited (BAMIC, modified Peetrons, Munich, Cohen, Chan and MLG-R) accounted for 70% of reports. Time to return to play was reported in 86% of studies; higher grades were linked to longer return times in reports for BAMIC (n = 12), modified Peetrons (n = 6), Munich (n = 6) and Cohen (n = 5), but the authors' Table 4 rates the evidence as conflicting for modified Peetrons and Cohen, and correlations appeared driven by extreme grades with limited value for intermediate grades. Good interrater reliability was reported for four classifications (kappa 0.80 to 1.00 for BAMIC, modified Peetrons and Chan; 0.82 to 1.00 for Munich), and validity was not reported for any classification.
paper.limitations: As a scoping review it did not critically appraise included studies, and the evidence is mostly low level. Only classifications with prognostic or return-to-play outcomes were included, so findings cannot be generalized to other muscle classifications. This copy is an accepted pre-proof without volume or page numbers, so the citation should be checked against the version of record.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a classification grade as one piece of information, since the authors conclude that classifications may help decision-making but are not accurate enough to predict time to return to play. When recording a muscle injury, state the classification and the return-to-play definition used (daily activity, training or competition), because the review shows these definitions vary widely.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff who track injury severity should use the same grading system and return-to-play definition across seasons so that data are comparable. The paper does not study performance outcomes, so its relevance here is limited to injury data quality.
paper.rtp: This review is directly relevant to return to play, but it does not set return dates or criteria. It supports using BAMIC, modified Peetrons, Munich and Cohen grades as descriptive tools with an inconsistent link to return time, notes that intermediate grades have limited prognostic value, and shows that validity was not reported for any classification. The authors call for a systematic review of evidence-based return-to-play criteria.
